## Introduction

This notebook is the narrative companion to the eight SQL EDA views in
`sql/02_eda_kupferkanne_2026.sql`. The split is deliberate: the views hold the
queryable, reproducible definitions; this document holds the reasoning built
on them - what the distributions look like, what was concluded, and how those
conclusions shaped the RFM transformation design
([ADR 0009](../docs/adr/0009-analytical-notebook-with-quarto.md)). Because the
pipeline runs EDA *between* validation and transformation
([ADR 0003](../docs/adr/0003-pipeline-order-eda-before-transform.md)), every
finding below preceded the segmentation design rather than justifying it after
the fact.

Each section follows the same shape: one distribution, one observation, and
the design decision that observation drove. A footer on every section maps the
finding to its ADR, its dashboard page, and its DAX measure family.

**Synthetic-data disclosure.** The dataset is generated by
[synth-datagen](https://github.com/ryszard-twardy/synth-datagen) with
intentional, documented quality issues (duplicate orders, cents-format
inconsistency, orphan keys, type drift - see
[ADR 0008](../docs/adr/0008-synthetic-data-with-realistic-quality-issues.md)).
The findings demonstrate method on realistic data; they are not market
insight about any real business.

::: {.callout-tip title="TL;DR - four findings"}
- **The top 20% of customers generate 71% of revenue** (the top decile alone
  carries 53%) - value-based segmentation is justified before a single
  segment is built.
- **Order values are hard right-skewed** (median EUR 35 vs mean EUR 51;
  1,679 orders sit beyond the P99 of EUR 268, the largest at 6.3x) -
  Monetary scoring must be quantile-based, not mean-based.
- **Only 26% of customers are single-order** - the Frequency dimension has
  enough spread for NTILE(5) quintiles to separate cleanly.
- **Germany carries 57% of revenue while average order value is flat
  (EUR 50 +/- 2%) across all nine markets** - market size, not basket
  economics, differentiates countries.
:::

### Reconciliation against the KPI baseline

Before trusting any chart below, the notebook proves it reads the same
universe as the dashboard and the KPI parity harness (`harness/`). Totals are
derived read-only from `sales_curated`; the population split across the EDA
views is stated and quantified, not assumed.

```{python}
#| label: setup
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
from decimal import Decimal
from google.cloud import bigquery
from IPython.display import HTML

PROJECT = "kupferkanne-2026"
DATASET = f"{PROJECT}.sales"
ACCENT = "#4A7AA0"
MUTED = "#C8CDD3"

client = bigquery.Client(project=PROJECT)


def view(name: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Read one EDA view into a DataFrame (read-only SELECT)."""
    sql = f"SELECT * FROM `{DATASET}.{name}`"
    return client.query(sql, location="EU").to_dataframe()


LABELS = {
    "recency_bucket": "Recency Bucket", "customer_count": "Customers",
    "min_days": "Min Days", "max_days": "Max Days", "order_id": "Order ID",
    "country": "Country", "order_value": "Order Value",
    "p99_threshold": "P99 Threshold", "multiple_of_p99": "Multiple of P99",
    "order_count": "Orders", "avg_order_value": "Avg Order Value",
    "total_revenue": "Total Revenue", "revenue_share_pct": "Revenue Share",
    "line_count": "Line Items", "avg_items_per_order": "Avg Items per Order",
    "avg_declared_items_per_order": "Avg Declared Items per Order",
    "declared_actual_mismatch_count": "Declared vs Actual Mismatch Count",
    "declared_actual_mismatch_pct": "Declared vs Actual Mismatch",
}


def show(df, labels=LABELS, percent=(), currency_int=(), ratio=()):
    """HTML table, no index. Formats float/Decimal cols (percent -> N.NN%,
    currency_int -> whole with thousands, ratio -> plain 2dp, else 2dp with
    thousands), then renames headers via `labels`."""
    out = df.copy()
    for col in out.columns:
        s = out[col]
        is_num = pd.api.types.is_float_dtype(s) or (
            s.dtype == object and s.map(lambda v: isinstance(v, Decimal)).any()
        )
        if col in percent:
            out[col] = s.map(lambda v: f"{float(v):.2f}%" if pd.notna(v) else "")
        elif col in currency_int:
            out[col] = s.map(lambda v: f"{float(v):,.0f}" if pd.notna(v) else "")
        elif col in ratio:
            out[col] = s.map(lambda v: f"{float(v):.2f}" if pd.notna(v) else "")
        elif is_num:
            out[col] = s.map(lambda v: f"{float(v):,.2f}" if pd.notna(v) else "")
    return HTML(out.rename(columns=labels).to_html(index=False))


plt.rcParams.update({
    "figure.figsize": (8, 3.5),
    "axes.spines.top": False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
    "axes.grid": True,
    "axes.grid.axis": "y",
    "grid.alpha": 0.3,
})
```

```{python}
#| label: reconciliation
BASELINE = {"Revenue": 8_531_365.52, "Orders": 168_777, "Customers": 14_967}

cur = client.query(
    f"""
    SELECT
        ROUND(SUM(order_value), 2) AS revenue,
        COUNT(*) AS orders,
        COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS customers
    FROM `{DATASET}.sales_curated`
    """,
    location="EU",
).to_dataframe().iloc[0]

derived = {
    "Revenue": round(float(cur["revenue"]), 2),
    "Orders": int(cur["orders"]),
    "Customers": int(cur["customers"]),
}

dist_orders = int(view("eda_order_value_distribution")["order_count"].iloc[0])
basket_orders = int(view("eda_basket_composition")["order_count"].sum())

recon = pd.DataFrame({
    "Metric": list(BASELINE),
    "KPI baseline": [f"{v:,.2f}" if isinstance(v, float) else f"{v:,}"
                     for v in BASELINE.values()],
    "Derived (sales_curated)": [f"{v:,.2f}" if isinstance(v, float)
                                else f"{v:,}" for v in derived.values()],
    "Match": ["yes" if BASELINE[k] == derived[k] else "NO"
              for k in BASELINE],
})
show(recon)
```

```{python}
#| label: population-split
split = pd.DataFrame({
    "Population": [
        "Item-bearing orders (order-value views, INNER JOIN - matches sales_curated)",
        "All validated orders (eda_basket_composition, LEFT JOIN)",
        "Delta: itemless orders (explained, not an error)",
    ],
    "Orders": [f"{dist_orders:,}", f"{basket_orders:,}",
               f"{basket_orders - dist_orders:,}"],
})
show(split)
```

The three headline totals match the baseline exactly. The population split is
the one reconciliation line that needs explaining: order-value views cover the
**168,777** item-bearing orders (INNER JOIN to item lines, the same population
as `sales_curated`), while the basket-composition view keeps all **169,181**
validated orders visible (LEFT JOIN) - the **404** itemless orders are a
seeded data-quality artifact examined in the Data quality section. A related
consequence: customer-grain views (frequency, recency) count 14,975 customers,
eight more than curated - those eight exist only through itemless orders.

## Recency

```{python}
#| label: fig-recency
#| fig-cap: "Customers by recency bucket, anchored on MAX(order_date) = the dataset's last order day."
#| fig-alt: "Bar chart of customer counts across six recency buckets, from active under 30 days (3,273 customers) to dormant beyond two years (1,413 customers)."
rec = view("eda_recency_distribution").sort_values("recency_bucket")
rec["customer_count"] = rec["customer_count"].astype(int)
labels = [b.split("_", 1)[1] for b in rec["recency_bucket"]]

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.bar(labels, rec["customer_count"], color=ACCENT)
ax.set_ylabel("Customers")
ax.set_xlabel("Recency bucket")
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-recency
show(rec[["recency_bucket", "customer_count", "min_days", "max_days"]])
```

The dataset ends in March 2026, so anchoring recency on `CURRENT_DATE()`
would add the same growing offset to every customer and compress the
distribution's low end into meaninglessness. Anchored on `MAX(order_date)`
instead, the spread is real and analytically useful: 3,273 customers ordered
within 30 days of the anchor, 6,928 within 90 days, and a long cold tail
remains - 2,335 customers between one and two years out, plus 1,413 dormant
beyond two years. That spread is what makes a Recency quintile worth
computing: NTILE(5) boundaries land on genuinely different behaviours rather
than slicing noise. The anchor decision was validated here before the RFM
pipeline hard-coded it. The bucket edges (30/90/180/365/730 days) also
prefigure the dashboard's recency bands used in churn analysis.

*Where this lands:* ADR 0006; Page 4 Churn Risk & What-If; Folder 04 - Time
Intelligence (Recency Buckets).

## Frequency

```{python}
#| label: fig-frequency
#| fig-cap: "Share of customers by lifetime order count (axis truncated at 20; the tail runs to 174 orders per customer)."
#| fig-alt: "Bar chart showing percentage of customers per order count. Single-order customers are the largest group at 26 percent, with a smooth declining tail."
freq = view("eda_customer_frequency_distribution").sort_values("order_count")
head = freq[freq["order_count"] <= 20].copy()
head["pct_of_customers"] = head["pct_of_customers"].astype(float)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.bar(head["order_count"].astype(int), head["pct_of_customers"], color=ACCENT)
ax.set_ylabel("% of customers")
ax.set_xlabel("Lifetime orders per customer")
ax.set_xticks(range(1, 21))
plt.show()
```

The failure mode this view exists to catch: if 80%+ of customers had exactly
one order, a Frequency quintile would be noise - four of five score bands
would slice a single behaviour. That did not materialise. Single-order
customers are 26.1% of the base; a customer at the median has roughly four
to five lifetime orders, and the tail stretches to 174 orders. With that
spread, NTILE(5) separates cleanly: the bottom quintile is not even fully
consumed by one-order customers, and each higher band captures a genuinely
more frequent behaviour. This is the observation that kept Frequency as a
full scoring dimension in the RFM design instead of collapsing it into a
binary repeat-buyer flag - an option that would have been correct under the
80% failure mode and wrong here.

*Where this lands:* ADR 0006; Page 2 Segment Deep Dive; Folder 02 - RFM
Scores.

## Monetary

```{python}
#| label: fig-monetary
#| fig-cap: "Order-value percentiles (EUR). The gap between P90 and P99 is the long tail."
#| fig-alt: "Bar chart of order value at percentiles 10, 25, 50, 75, 90 and 99, rising steeply from about 11 euros at P10 to 268 euros at P99."
dist = view("eda_order_value_distribution").iloc[0]
pct_labels = ["p10", "p25", "median", "p75", "p90", "p99"]
pct_values = [float(dist[c]) for c in pct_labels]

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.bar([p.upper() for p in pct_labels], pct_values, color=ACCENT)
ax.set_ylabel("Order value (EUR)")
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-outliers
out = view("eda_order_value_outliers")
out = out.sort_values("order_value", ascending=False).head(5)
show(out[["order_id", "country", "order_value", "p99_threshold", "multiple_of_p99"]], ratio=["multiple_of_p99"])
```

The shape is hard right-skew: median EUR 35.03 against a mean of EUR 50.55,
P90 at EUR 105 and P99 at EUR 267.54, with a maximum of EUR 1,694 - 6.3x the
P99 threshold. 1,679 orders (just under 1%) sit beyond P99. Inspected, the
tail reads as legitimate high-value or B2B-style baskets rather than
artifacts: values are plausible multiples, spread across markets, and the
cents-format errors that would fake such a tail were already normalised in
cleaning. Two consequences: Monetary scoring must be quantile-based (a
mean-anchored split would put the boundary above 60% of orders), and the
whales must stay in - they are exactly whom the Champions segment exists to
identify. Order value here is the curated expression verbatim -
`ROUND(SUM(line_net_amount), 2)` per order, items INNER JOINed, discount not
applied - so every figure reconciles with `sales_curated`.

*Where this lands:* ADR 0006; Page 2 Segment Deep Dive; Folder 02 - RFM
Scores.

## Temporal pattern

```{python}
#| label: fig-temporal
#| fig-cap: "Monthly revenue, January 2023 to March 2026 (39 months; final month truncated at the data cutoff)."
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of monthly revenue over 39 months, ramping up through 2023, peaking each December with a maximum of about 789 thousand euros in December 2024, and dropping in the truncated final month."
mon = view("eda_monthly_temporal_pattern").sort_values("year_month")
mon["monthly_revenue"] = mon["monthly_revenue"].astype(float)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(mon["year_month"], mon["monthly_revenue"], color=ACCENT, linewidth=2)
ax.set_ylabel("Monthly revenue (EUR)")
ax.set_xticks(mon["year_month"][::6])
plt.show()
```

Thirty-nine months, three regimes. A 2023 ramp-up as the synthetic customer
base accumulates; a mature phase with pronounced December peaks (the maximum,
EUR 789K, lands in December 2024); and a final month visibly truncated -
March 2026 stops mid-month at the data cutoff. None of this is a market
finding (the seasonality is generator-encoded), but two analytical handling
decisions hang on it. First, the bounded panel is precisely why recency is
anchored on `MAX(order_date)`: the dataset's "now" is March 2026, not the
render date. Second, the truncated final month is a known hazard for any
month-over-month comparison downstream - the dashboard's time series
inherits it, and a naive last-month delta would read as a collapse. The gaps
check also passes: all 39 calendar months are present, so temporal coverage
is continuous.

*Where this lands:* ADR 0006 (anchor); Page 1 Executive Summary; Folder 01 -
Core KPIs.

## Geography

```{python}
#| label: fig-geography
#| fig-cap: "Revenue share by customer country (customer-grain attribution, matching sales_curated)."
#| fig-alt: "Bar chart of revenue share for nine countries, dominated by Germany at 57 percent, followed by Austria at 12 percent and Poland at 8 percent."
geo = view("eda_country_breakdown").sort_values("total_revenue",
                                                ascending=False)
geo["revenue_share_pct"] = geo["revenue_share_pct"].astype(float)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.bar(geo["country"], geo["revenue_share_pct"], color=ACCENT)
ax.set_ylabel("Revenue share (%)")
ax.set_xlabel("Country")
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-geography
show(geo[["country", "order_count", "customer_count", "avg_order_value",
     "total_revenue", "revenue_share_pct"]], currency_int=["total_revenue"], percent=["revenue_share_pct"])
```

Germany dominates with 56.8% of revenue; the top three markets (DE, AT, PL)
carry 77%. The more interesting observation is what does *not* vary: average
order value sits in a band from EUR 49.72 (UK) to EUR 51.43 (SE) - under
3.5% spread across nine markets. Market differences are volume differences,
not basket-economics differences, which means country is a scale attribute
for segmentation, not a behavioural one - RFM scores need no per-country
normalisation. One semantic note inherited from the curated layer: country
is the *customer's* country (joined from `v_dim_customers_std` at customer
grain), not a shipping attribute of the order, and customers with no country
on the dimension would surface as NULL rather than being relabelled.

*Where this lands:* ADR 0014 (Deneb regional map); Page 6 Regional Analysis;
Folder 06 - Formatting & Regional.

## Concentration

```{python}
#| label: fig-concentration
#| fig-cap: "Cumulative revenue share by customer revenue decile (decile 1 = highest-spending 10%)."
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of cumulative revenue share across ten customer deciles, reaching 53 percent after the first decile, 71 percent after the second, and flattening toward 100 percent."
par = view("eda_pareto_concentration").sort_values("revenue_decile")
par["pct_of_total_revenue"] = par["pct_of_total_revenue"].astype(float)
cum = par["pct_of_total_revenue"].cumsum()

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(par["revenue_decile"].astype(int), cum, color=ACCENT, linewidth=2,
        marker="o")
ax.axhline(80, color=MUTED, linestyle="--", linewidth=1)
ax.set_ylabel("Cumulative revenue share (%)")
ax.set_xlabel("Customer revenue decile")
ax.set_xticks(range(1, 11))
ax.set_ylim(0, 105)
plt.show()
```

The top decile of customers generates 53.4% of revenue; the top two deciles
together, 71.1%. The canonical 80/20 rule does not quite hold - the top 20%
carry 71%, and reaching 80% takes the top three deciles - but the strategic
conclusion survives the nuance: revenue concentration is steep enough that
value-tiered treatment (retention spend on Champions, win-back on
high-value At Risk) is justified, while the curve is shallow enough that the
bottom half is not economically irrelevant (it still carries ~10%). This
view validated the segmentation *ex ante*, before any segment existed; the
dashboard's revenue-concentration chart on Page 5 monitors the same curve
*ex post*, per segment, as the data evolves. The two are complements, not
duplicates.

*Where this lands:* ADR 0006; Page 5 Customer Lifecycle Intelligence
(Revenue Concentration / Pareto); Folder 03 - Segment Analysis.

## Data quality

```{python}
#| label: fig-quality
#| fig-cap: "Share of orders whose declared basket size disagrees with the actual item-line count, by country."
#| fig-alt: "Bar chart of declared versus actual mismatch percentage for nine countries, all between 0.44 and 0.75 percent."
bas = view("eda_basket_composition").sort_values(
    "declared_actual_mismatch_pct", ascending=False)
bas["declared_actual_mismatch_pct"] = (
    bas["declared_actual_mismatch_pct"].astype(float))

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.bar(bas["country"], bas["declared_actual_mismatch_pct"], color=ACCENT)
ax.set_ylabel("Mismatch (% of orders)")
ax.set_xlabel("Country")
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-quality
show(bas[["country", "order_count", "line_count", "avg_items_per_order",
     "avg_declared_items_per_order", "declared_actual_mismatch_count",
     "declared_actual_mismatch_pct"]], percent=["declared_actual_mismatch_pct"])
```

Every order arrives with a declared basket size (`basket_item_count`); the
view cross-checks it against the actual item-line count. The two disagree on
0.65% of orders overall (1,092 of 169,181), in a narrow 0.44-0.75% band per
country - trace-level residue of the quality issues ADR 0008 deliberately
seeds, surviving past cleaning at exactly the magnitude a real warehouse
would show. The uniformity across countries matters: a systematic grain
error (say, declared counts meaning units while actual counts mean lines)
would produce mismatch rates near 100%, not below 1%. This is also where the
404 itemless orders from the reconciliation live - kept visible by the LEFT
JOIN with an actual count of zero, because hiding them would hide precisely
the mismatches the view exists to catch. Basket size itself is flat across
markets (1.60-1.63 lines per order), consistent with the geography finding.

*Where this lands:* ADR 0008; pipeline step `01_0` (cleaning/validation);
no dashboard page or DAX measure family consumes this view directly - it is
an EDA-only data-quality check.

## Synthesis

| Observation | Design decision | ADR |
|---|---|---|
| Right-skewed order values (median EUR 35 vs mean EUR 51; P99 EUR 268) | Quantile-based Monetary scoring; whales retained, not trimmed | [0006](../docs/adr/0006-rfm-segmentation-with-ntile.md) |
| Only 26% of customers are single-order | Frequency kept as a full NTILE(5) dimension, not a repeat-buyer flag | [0006](../docs/adr/0006-rfm-segmentation-with-ntile.md) |
| Bounded panel ending March 2026 | Recency anchored on `MAX(order_date)`, not `CURRENT_DATE()` | [0006](../docs/adr/0006-rfm-segmentation-with-ntile.md) |
| Top 20% of customers carry 71% of revenue | Value-tiered segment actions ex ante; Page 5 Pareto monitors ex post | [0006](../docs/adr/0006-rfm-segmentation-with-ntile.md) |
| Findings needed *before* transform design | Pipeline order: audit, clean, validate, **EDA**, transform | [0003](../docs/adr/0003-pipeline-order-eda-before-transform.md) |
| 0.65% declared-vs-actual mismatch; 404 itemless orders | Seeded DQ issues give cleaning real work; residue quantified, not hidden | [0008](../docs/adr/0008-synthetic-data-with-realistic-quality-issues.md) |
| Flat AOV (EUR 50 +/- 2%) across nine markets | No per-country normalisation of RFM scores | [0006](../docs/adr/0006-rfm-segmentation-with-ntile.md) |

The through-line: every structural choice in the RFM pipeline - quintile
scoring, the recency anchor, keeping the whales, treating geography as scale
rather than behaviour - traces back to a distribution inspected on this page.
Nothing above is a new claim; each row consolidates a finding argued in its
section, and the ADRs hold the durable record.

## Appendix: Reproduce this analysis

Rendering queries BigQuery live; the published HTML does not - a reader of
the rendered report needs no credentials. To re-render:

1. **Prerequisites** (machine-local, not covered by the repo manifest):
   Quarto CLI (1.9+), Google Cloud SDK with Application Default Credentials
   (`gcloud auth application-default login`) and read access to the
   `kupferkanne-2026.sales` dataset.
2. **Python environment** (covered by the manifest): `uv sync` at the repo
   root reproduces the full environment (`pyproject.toml` + `uv.lock`).
3. **Render** (PowerShell, from the repo root):

```powershell
$env:QUARTO_PYTHON = ".venv\Scripts\python.exe"
quarto render notebooks/eda_kupferkanne.qmd
```

Caching note: Quarto's `freeze` (render caching) requires a Quarto *project*
(`_quarto.yml`). This repository now defines one - added so the notebook
publishes to GitHub Pages - so the prerequisite is met; `freeze` itself stays
disabled for a single document and can be enabled if more notebooks accumulate.
